label: prf:operator-selection-lp
title: Proof of operator selection lp
html:
The feasible set is non-empty: any element \Phi_0 with \mathrm{tr}_M(\Phi_0) > 0 can be rescaled to satisfy the net constraint, and the Frobenius positivity constraints admit interior points (the identity \gamma = \mathbf{1} satisfies G \cdot e_1 > 0 componentwise for generic q). The boundedness constraint x_i \geq -M ensures the feasible polyhedron is bounded. By the LP strong duality theorem (no duality gap for feasible, bounded linear programs), the primal minimum equals the dual maximum.

Complementary slackness

At optimality, the complementary slackness conditions hold:

  y_i^* \cdot \left(\sum_{j=1}^{d} G_{ij}\, x_j^* \right) = 0
  \quad \forall\, i

Each dual variable y_i^* is positive only when the corresponding Frobenius constraint is tight. The set of tight constraints \mathcal{A} = \{i : y_i^* > 0\} identifies the active demand channels -- the channels that the optimal operator \Phi^* exactly saturates.

Higher-strand generalizations

For n > 3, the LP dimensions grow as d = n!:

n d = n! Physical regime
2 2 Single-particle states (photon, electron)
3 6 Baryonic confinement (proton, neutron)
4 24 Tetraquark / exotic meson candidates
5 120 Pentaquark states

At each strand number, the Frobenius Gram matrix G is symmetric, and it is non-degenerate — for q \neq 0, 1 — on the quotient H_n/\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{tr}_M \cong \mathrm{TL}_n, not on H_n itself, so that is where the LP is well-posed.

The LP dimension is the Catalan number C_n, not n!. Posed on all of H_n with d = n! the statement above is false: at z = q^3/(q^2+1) the weights y_\lambda vanish for every \lambda with \ell(\lambda) \geq 3, so G \in \mathbb{R}^{n! \times n!} is singular and the LP is degenerate rather than well-posed. Its rank is the surviving \sum \dim^2 = C_n:

n d = n! (as tabled) \mathrm{rank} G = C_n corank
2 2 2 0
3 6 5 1
4 24 14 10 = 3^2 + 1^2
5 120 42 78 = 6^2+5^2+4^2+1^2

So the pentaquark row is a 42-dimensional program, not a 120-dimensional one, and the tetraquark row is 14, not 24. The optimal vertex x^* and the active set \mathcal{A} are well defined on the quotient; on H_n the LP has a \mathrm{corank} G-dimensional space of optima differing by radical directions the trace cannot see.

The optimal vertex x^* identifies the minimum-action operator, and the active set \mathcal{A} identifies the saturated demand channels.

Relation to the spectral decomposition

The spectral decomposition writes \Phi = \sum_\lambda d_\lambda(q) \cdot \Phi_\lambda in the irrep basis; the LP writes \Phi = \sum_i x_i b_i in the NF basis. The two are related by the change-of-basis matrix P between the NF basis and the Wedderburn idempotent basis:

  x_i = \sum_\lambda P_{i\lambda} \, d_\lambda(q) \,
  \mathrm{tr}_\lambda(\Phi_\lambda)

The LP operates in the NF basis because the Gram matrix G_{ij} and the Markov traces t_i are directly computable from the Hecke algebra relations, without requiring explicit knowledge of the irrep decomposition. The spectral decomposition provides the physical interpretation (which knot operators mediate the interaction); the LP provides the constructive selection (which NF coefficients minimize the action).
